# Loop trace

```
Automated tests ──(−)──▶ Bugs reaching users ──(+)──▶ Urgent hotfixes
      ▲                                                      │
      │                                                     (−)
     (+)                                                     │
      └────────────── Time to write tests ◀─────────────────┘
```

| Link | Direction | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Tests → Bugs reaching users | **−** (opposite) | More tests means fewer bugs |
| Bugs reaching users → Urgent hotfixes | **+** (same) | More bugs means more hotfixes |
| Urgent hotfixes → Time to write tests | **−** (opposite) | Hotfixes take time away from writing tests |
| Time to write tests → Tests | **+** (same) | More time means more tests |

**Polarity check:** the loop has two negative links (an even number), so it is **reinforcing**.

## Label: **R – "Test Virtuous Cycle"**

It is also known as the **firefighting trap** when it runs in reverse. A reinforcing loop amplifies change in whichever direction it starts:

- **Virtuous direction:** more tests lead to fewer bugs, which means fewer hotfixes. That frees up time, which produces still more tests.
- **Vicious direction:** few tests lead to more bugs, which means more hotfixes. That leaves no time for tests, so the team ends up with even fewer tests.

## Notes
- **The starting point matters.** A team already stuck in the vicious direction usually needs a deliberate intervention to flip it. One example is protecting dedicated test time, or pausing feature work for a sprint.
- **The loop won't grow forever.** Diminishing returns on bug prevention and the maintenance cost of the tests will eventually limit it. Those limits would be balancing loops (B) that cap the growth.
- **Something is missing from the model.** New feature work also competes for the same time, and it can introduce new bugs. Adding it would show why the loop often stalls in practice.
